title: Imagine the moment.
paragraphs: Imagine the moment.

The desert wind is blowing across the camp of Israel.
Dust moves between thousands of tents.
Fires crackle. Children cry. People shout.
But something is terribly wrong.
Snakes are everywhere.
Venomous serpents have entered the camp, and people are collapsing in the sand.

Men who walked through the Red Sea…
Women who watched manna fall from heaven…
Now lie dying in the wilderness.
The story is recorded in Book of Numbers 21:4–9.
And it begins with something painfully human.
Complaining.
The people began to speak against God and against Moses.
“Why have you brought us out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread! There is no water! And we detest this miserable food.”

They were tired.
They were frustrated.
They were ungrateful.
And their hearts turned against the very God who had rescued them.
So the Bible says the Lord allowed venomous serpents to enter the camp.

People were bitten.
Many died.
Suddenly the complaining stopped.
Panic replaced it.
The people ran to Moses and cried out:
“We sinned when we spoke against the Lord.”
This is one of the most important moments in the story.
They didn’t blame circumstances.
They confessed their sin.
And Moses prayed for them.
Then God gave a command that must have sounded strange.
“Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole. Anyone who is bitten can look at it and live.”
Think about that.
God did not remove every snake.
He did not instantly heal everyone.
Instead, He gave them something to look at.
Moses made a serpent of bronze and lifted it high above the camp.
Anyone who had been bitten could look at it…
…and live.
The cure looked like the very thing that was killing them.
But the power wasn’t in the bronze.
The power was in obedient faith.
A dying person didn’t have to crawl miles.
They didn’t have to perform a ritual.
They didn’t have to prove their worth.
They simply had to look where God told them to look.
And if they did…
the poison lost its power.
But the story doesn’t end in the desert.
Hundreds of years later, Jesus Christ revealed the deeper meaning of that moment.
In Gospel of John 3:14–15, Jesus said:
“Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life.”
This was not just a miracle.
It was a prophecy.
The bronze serpent represented the curse that was killing the people.
Yet the symbol of the curse was lifted up as the place of healing.
In the same way, Jesus was lifted up on the cross carrying the weight of human sin.
Scripture says in Second Epistle to the Corinthians 5:21 that God made Him who knew no sin to become sin for us.
The sinless One carried the curse so that those who look to Him in faith could live.
Just like the Israelites.
They didn’t defeat the snakes.
They didn’t neutralize the venom.
They simply looked at what God lifted up.
And they lived.
That same principle still echoes through the gospel today.
Many people try to fix themselves first.
They try to become perfect before turning to God.
They try to earn forgiveness.
But the gospel was never about earning life.
It is about looking to the One who was lifted up.
The cross stands in history the same way the bronze serpent stood in the desert.
Visible.
Unavoidable.
And full of mercy.
Three truths stand out in this story.

First:
Sin spreads like venom. Quietly. Quickly. Fatally.

Second:
God’s rescue sometimes looks unexpected before it reveals its power.

Third:
Life comes when we look in faith where God tells us to look.
The Israelites looked at a bronze serpent and lived physically.
But those who look to Christ receive something even greater.

Forgiveness.
Restoration.
Eternal life.
The desert miracle healed bodies.
The cross heals souls.
And the invitation is still the same today.
Look.
And live.
Now a question for you:

If you had been in that camp…
bitten… weak… dying…
would you have believed enough to look?
Or would pride, doubt, or disbelief have kept your eyes down?
Because sometimes the difference between life and death…
is simply looking where God told you to look.

Numbers 21:8–9
John 3:14–15
What lesson do you see in the story of the bronze serpent?
